title: Children
hookLine: five ways parents care for a child, and not one hug on the list (DN 31)
tomorrow: teach a child the rules first, or teach them to ask? two old answers.

cards: Parenting advice arrives in a flood now: screen-time charts, gentle scripts for meltdowns, the one phrase never to say. The Buddha's version is short.
In the advice to Sigala, the Sigalovada, there's a list of five ways parents care for a child. Read it slowly and something's odd. Keep them from what's harmful.
Settle them in what's good. Train them in a skill. Help them toward a fitting marriage.
Hand over what they'll inherit, at the right time. No hugs. No praise.

teach.b: Start with where parents stand in this teaching. The Sigalovada maps a life onto six directions, and parents are the east, where the day begins. The list isn't about how a child feels this afternoon.
It's about where the child is headed.
The first two lines carry the weight: away from harm, toward good. A parent here is a guide on a road, not an entertainer.

teach.h: A SKILL, A PARTNER, A HANDOVER.
teach.b: The next three walk a child out into adult life: a skill to earn by, a partner when the time comes, and an inheritance handed over, not held back. Look at the shape. It ends with the parent letting go of what's theirs.

The marriage line sounds strange to modern ears, and families today read it in different ways; in its world, a family helped a young person into adult life. The thread is a launch, not control. Is it cold?
The text frames all five as the ways parents care. The warmth is in the steering.

teach.h: THE GRAB AT THE HOT PAN.
teach.b: Anyone who has caught a small hand reaching for a hot pan knows that grab is love, though nobody claps for it.
And the road has two lanes. The same passage lists what a child gives back. So the answer to the puzzle: the guiding is the love.

how: Buddhist parents and teachers often point to the Sigalovada when they talk about raising children: steering them from harm toward good, giving them a skill, and handing over in time.

o: the ones parents steer from harm toward good, then let go
the ones who must obey without asking, in the old order
the ones parents keep happy and close for their whole lives

games.q: the parents' list — tap the pairs.
p: the east, where the day begins
something to earn a living by
handed over at the right time

s: the Sigalovada says a parent's first job is to keep a child happy
its list opens with keeping them from harm and settling them in good.
in the Sigalovada, the duties between parent and child run both ways
the same passage lists what a child gives back to the parents.
the list ends with the parent holding on to the family's wealth
it ends with handing the inheritance over, at the right time.

games.q: you're watching a friend's kid. they ask, sweetly, for a third cookie and the tablet right before dinner. what's guiding them, in the Sigalovada's sense?
o: say yes to both; a happy kid is the whole point of the afternoon.
no to both, then nothing else; holding the line is the guiding.
no to the tablet, and hand them a real job: help set the table.
games.why: the list pairs away-from-harm with toward-good. a no with nothing after it is only half the guiding.

practice: Think of one child in your life: your own, a niece, a neighbor's kid, a student, or the child you once were. Choose one good thing you could teach them, small and real: how to say sorry, how to crack an egg, how to wait a turn.
Run through the teaching slowly in your mind, and watch the face that learns it.

wordCard.voice: Children: in the Sigalovada, the ones parents steer away from harm and toward good, then launch, then let go.

orig.note: Pali: compassion, caring for someone; the sense of how parents care in the passage.

carryVoice: Here's the line: guide them, and the steering is the love. Eight of eleven, still on family.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 31 (Sigalovada Sutta: parents as the eastern direction; the five ways parents care for a child: restraining from evil, settling in good, training in a skill or profession, arranging a suitable marriage, handing over the inheritance in due time; the child's five duties in return)
